text: that MRSA is becoming more prevalent in the community.1-5 Guidelines for the control of MRSA are available in many countries.6 In the UK, revised guidelines7 for the control of MRSA in healthcare facilities were produced by a joint working party of the British Society for Antimicrobial Chemotherapy, the Hospital Infection Society, and the In- fection Control Nurses Association in 2006. They advise prompt isolation of infected or colonised patients, screen- ing of patients and staff in contact with such patients, the use of protective clothing, handwashing with an antiseptic detergent, and the use by all patients of an antiseptic deter- gent for washing and bathing. For eradication of nasal car- riage they recommend mupirocin nasal ointment. Eradica- tion at other colonised sites is more difficult: antiseptic detergents may be used for skin and hair washing. A sys- tematic review8 has concluded that there is insufficient ev- idence to support the use of topical or systemic antimicro- bial therapy for eradicating nasal or extra-nasal MRSA. Although ciprofloxacin may be used the emergence of widespread resistance in meticillin-sensitive and meticil- lin-resistant Staph. aureus limits its usefulness (see p.246). Combination therapy may be helpful. Rifampicin is highly active against MRSA, but it must always be used with an- other drug to prevent the emergence of resistance. Combi- nations of rifampicin with gentamicin, vancomycin, co-tri- moxazole, fusidic acid, quinolones, or novobiocin have been tried. Newer antibacterials such as daptomycin, line- zolid, or quinupristin/dalfopristin may be effective and may assume increasing importance. Isolated reports from around the world of MRSA with in- termediate resistance or reduced susceptibility to vanco- mycin initially emerged in the late 1990s,9-11 and in re- sponse the CDC produced interim12 and later13 guidelines for preventing the spread of vancomycin-intermediate Staph. aureus (VISA) and vancomycin-resistant Staph. aureus (VRSA). Staphylococcal vaccines have been used for the prophy- laxis and treatment of staphylococcal infections.
